findings.title: Deauthentication / disassociation flood
findings.detail: 16 deauth-class frames from 04:42:1a:19:88:f8 inside a 5-second window -- the signature of a forced disconnect, used either as denial of service or to make a client reconnect so its four-way handshake can be captured
evidence: 20 frames total, peak 16 within 5 s starting at t+11.03 s
reason codes seen: 7 (class 3 frame received from nonassociated STA)
0/20 frames were cryptographically protected
none were protected, so every one of them is forgeable by any device in range
findings.benign_explanation: an access point rebooting, shedding clients under load, or steering a client to another band also emits deauths, though rarely this many this fast from one address

findings.title: Complete four-way handshake captured
findings.detail: the full handshake between 56:09:29:8d:dc:1f and 04:42:1a:19:88:f8 ("testnetworkRPT88") is in this capture. WPA2 derives the PTK from the PMK and the two nonces with no key exchange, so recovering the passphrase later decrypts this session retroactively -- WPA2-PSK has no forward secrecy
evidence: completed in 24.7 ms
ANonce 97cdbe26f045e49b...
SNonce 536b3bc34104bd41...
remediation: WPA3-SAE runs a Dragonfly key exchange per session, so a later passphrase compromise reveals nothing

findings.title: Unprotected deauth on an MFP-required network
findings.detail: "testnetworkRPT88" (04:42:1a:19:88:f8) requires management frame protection, so compliant clients will ignore these unprotected frames -- the attack is visible but ineffective
evidence: RSN capabilities: MFP required
